title: Buying Taste, Not Things
sentences: What people buy has always signalled who they are, or who they would like to appear to be.
Owning fewer, better objects now functions as its own quiet boast among the comfortably well off.
Minimalism, ostensibly a rejection of excess, can be just another costly aesthetic to maintain.
The empty shelf and the plain mug both had to be chosen, priced, and, in some sense, performed.
Meanwhile, taste itself has become a kind of currency, traded in glances rather than coins.
To notice the right object at the right moment marks a person as belonging to a certain class.
This is not new, but it has grown subtler, dressed in the language of restraint and simplicity.
A cluttered home once suggested poverty; now it can just as easily suggest a lack of discipline.
And yet the urge beneath both clutter and restraint remains the same desire to be judged well.
To shop, then, is rarely only to acquire; it is to rehearse a story about oneself for others.
Whether that story is true hardly matters, so long as the audience finds it convincing enough.
